source.title: NG+ : A Multi-Step Matrix-Product Natural Gradient Method for Deep Learning
source.authors: Minghan Yang; Dong Xu; Qiwen Cui; Zai-Wen Wen; Peng-Xiang Xu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; minor OCR/typesetting corruption is visible in equations, but the experimental sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training and held-out performance for several tasks and optimizer comparisons, but does not test memorization of random labels or the mapped generalization mechanisms. Its experiments use a stopping rule based on held-out accuracy and its large-batch results are explicitly preliminary, so they do not establish the proposed claim broadly.
record.gate_note: The ImageNet experiment reports training and testing accuracy over time, but terminates methods when they reach a target test accuracy; the large-batch comparison reports only epochs and iterations. Other tasks report validation/test performance or training and test metrics, but do not compare train-test gaps under the claim's specified conditions. The methods and results cited from other studies are not this paper's own results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates NG+ optimization performance but provides no interpretable test of a claim version. The ImageNet Adam result is omitted with an unspecified statement of poor performance; this does not identify worse held-out performance relative to SGD. Batch-size comparisons report epochs to a shared accuracy target with different recipes, rather than held-out performance under a fixed epoch budget.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors present NG+ as a promising matrix-product natural-gradient method, establish convergence and online regret guarantees under assumptions, and report competitive numerical performance across four application areas. They identify comprehensive large-batch evaluation as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and evaluates NG+, a multi-step matrix-product natural-gradient optimizer; it does not reproduce the random-label, width-sweep, architecture, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example interventions in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: For ResNet50/ImageNet, batch sizes 256, 2048, and 4096 are reported, but held-out results for the large-batch settings are not given. Optimizer results vary by task and metric: NG+ reaches a target test accuracy on ImageNet, has higher reported BLEU than Adam on IWSLT14, and is compared with Adam on SchNet validation loss.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet50/ImageNet reaches 75.9% test accuracy in 76 epochs with SGD, 74 with LARS, 42 with KFAC, and 40 with NG+. Methods stop at the accuracy target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NG+ reaches a specified ImageNet accuracy faster than the tested alternatives.

fits_no_version.finding: NG+ takes 40 epochs at batch size 256 and 41 epochs at sizes 2048 and 4096 under the shared accuracy stopping rule. Learning rates, schedules, and damping differ across batch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With batch-specific recipes, NG+ reaches the ImageNet accuracy target in nearly the same number of epochs across these batch sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: NG+ and Adam achieve Transformer test BLEU of 34.79 ± 0.09 and 34.75 ± 0.08, respectively, over three runs; NG+ has lower training loss. This comparison contains no SGD baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NG+ and Adam obtain similar reported translation BLEU in this experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: SchNet comparisons emphasize validation-loss convergence speed; DLRM best test accuracy is 79.175% with NG+ versus 79.149% with AdaGrad.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NG+ offers task-specific optimization and predictive-performance advantages over the tested methods.

record.problems: The ImageNet comparison stops each method at a target test accuracy, limiting comparison of final generalization gaps. The large-batch ImageNet table reports only epochs and iterations. Several results are presented in figures without numeric values in the text. Adam's ImageNet result is omitted because the authors say it does not perform well.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows. ImageNet batch-size results in Table 2 report only epochs and iterations, not held-out accuracy; ImageNet optimizer results stop at a shared test-accuracy threshold. Figure-only curves do not provide a stated gap outcome suitable for the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy with the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance under comparable limited or broader tuning. Adam's unspecified poor ImageNet performance does not establish a generalization disadvantage.
Held-out performance across batch sizes at a fixed epoch budget, including whether recipe changes remove a penalty.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: There are no extracted rows to correct. The record already declares the omitted optimizer curves and batch-size statistics in rows_left_out. Neither a train-test gap nor an exact numeric value is universally required for these versions, but the reported comparisons must still identify the behavior and conditions the version names.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels under the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.

Whether adaptive optimizers generalize worse than SGD under comparable tuning; the paper reports that Adam performs poorly on ResNet50/ImageNet without providing a result suitable for a direct held-out comparison.
Whether large batches worsen held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets; the paper provides only epoch and iteration counts for the large-batch settings.
Dropout and its effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
